content: To ensure that surveillance results are actionable for public health interventions, it is critical that they provide an up-to-date representation of the HIV epidemic. This can only be achieved if the results are disseminated promptly. The sample size required for estimating a single prevalence proportion in sentinel surveillance is determined by the assumed prevalence level and the desired precision of the estimate. Under simple random sampling with replacement, the approximate confidence interval around a prevalence proportion (ρ) is calculated using the formula: Z(1-α/2)√(ρ(1-ρ)/η), where η represents the sample size, Z(1-α/2) is the Z-score corresponding to the significance level, and ρ is the estimated proportion of HIV-positive individuals. For a 95% confidence interval, α is set to 0.05. The margin of error (d) is half the width of the confidence interval and is given by the same formula. The sample size for simple random sampling (SRS) can then be approximated as SRS = Z(1-α/2)²ρ(1-ρ)/d². When monitoring changes in prevalence over time, the required sample size depends on the statistical measure used to express change and the precision required. Two common measures are the absolute difference in prevalence between two time points and the ratio of prevalence estimates at two time points. For example, the difference in prevalence (Δρ) is calculated as ρt ρt-Δt, where t represents the time of the initial survey and Δt is the survey interval. The ratio of prevalence estimates is expressed as ρt/ρt-Δt. The sample size required to estimate these changes with a specified confidence interval can be calculated using similar statistical methods. In countries where HIV prevalence is decreasing, a conservative sample size estimate can be obtained by assuming constant prevalence. The design-adjusted sample size is then calculated as η × DEFF × r, where DEFF is the design effect, and r is the fraction of sampling units expected to provide complete data. For young pregnant women (aged 15–24 years) in sentinel surveillance, two approaches can be used to control the precision of prevalence estimates: inflation and oversampling. The inflation method involves increasing the sample size to ensure adequate representation of young pregnant women. For example, if the unadjusted sample size is 300 and young pregnant women are expected to comprise 32% of the sample, the inflated sample size would be 300/0.32 = 938. Oversampling, on the other hand, involves calculating separate sample sizes for all eligible pregnant women (aged 15–49 years) and for young pregnant women. Sampling continues until the overall target is met, after which only young pregnant women are sampled until their target is reached. This approach is more complex and requires close monitoring of surveillance data and separate analyses for different populations. Statistical models are essential for analyzing trends in HIV prevalence as they filter out random variations and reveal the effects of key factors. Logistic regression is commonly used for trend analysis, as it models prevalence on the logit scale, which is confined to the interval [0,1]. Linear trends on the logit scale correspond to curvilinear trends on the prevalence scale. Mixed-effects logistic regression models can account for site-specific random effects and provide estimates of site-specific and overall trends. These models can be implemented using statistical software such as SAS, Stata, or R. Sentinel surveillance data collection forms typically include sociodemographic information, HIV testing and treatment status, and syphilis testing and treatment information. These forms are designed to capture comprehensive data for monitoring and evaluating the HIV epidemic and related public health interventions.
